rv.q: An exquisite portrait of 21st-century Americana, centering on a family divided by politics, ideology and a hidden history, “Other Desert Cities” is smart, authentic and deeply satisfying.
It’s still the juicy banger of a dysfunctional family play by Jon Robin Baitz, a delicious feast of schadenfreude.
The show has become a scorchingly hot ticket—hotter, you might say, than asphalt on an August day in the Southern California city of Palm Springs, where the play is set.
A decade and a half after its premiere, this revival makes a strong case for its ranking among the better of those, and a definitive one for its dissection of American rot – perhaps too eerily.
Baitz’ play seems just as vital in today’s bitterly divisive political and social environment.
Louis-Dreyfus has crashed at last into Broadway.

Witty, bitter, flamboyant, and emotionally grounded, the dialogue swings, delightfully, between intimate exchanges and grandiloquent soliloquies, capturing the vulnerability of idealists in the face of evil.
But the likeable enough Broadway revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s sharp-tongued drama, which opened Sunday night at the Hudson Theatre, takes these people’s competing personalities way too far.
“Other Desert Cities” was written for another era, and this revival’s moderating influence only underscores just how much things have degenerated between now and then.
But if you ask me, anyone willing to pay that much for a basically middling production will be getting what they deserve.
Just about everything else in this expensively populated place is arid, overheated and woefully devoid of life.
If only these actors could dedicate themselves to material more worthy of all our time.
Mr. Baitz’s play provides both robust entertainment and much-needed moral nourishment — as opposed to pat judgment, which is precisely what this equally witty and moving piece decries.

Under John Benjamin Hickey’s deft direction, a stellar five-person ensemble made up of Louis-Dreyfus, Allison Janney, Ed Harris, Lily Rabe and Joe Keery brings humor, humanity and devastating emotional depth to a crackling revival that feels strikingly relevant in 2026.
Baitz doesn’t do average—everything rises and falls on razor-sharp dialogue and cunningly crafted scenes.
The Seinfeld alum steals the show from the second the action begins, making her Broadway debut a rousing success.
It’s a first-rate production, in many ways better than the original.
It speaks to the power of Baitz’s play that the core tragedy works brilliantly with two such different interpretations of Polly Wyeth.

The cast certainly knocks it out of the park in this production directed by actor John Bejamin Hickey, who scored a similar commercial triumph with his staging of Neil Simon’s Plaza Suite at the same theater.
This Desert is still an entertaining and moving evening (it better be at those astronomical prices, with top seats going for four figures).
Conversely, Rabe is consistently mesmerizing, proving why Brooke is the true fulcrum of this unbalanced tale.
All of this gives the conclusion of Other Desert Cities a depressing kind of resonance, if perhaps not the kind its creators intended.
So all I’ll say about the ending is that it drives home the apolitical nature of a play that only appears to be political.

What should be a ferocious cage match instead feels like a bowling tournament with the bumpers up: Yes, everyone is trying their damnedest, but the fireworks sputter out before they can ever really ignite.
But the cast, while stacked, doesn’t have the chemistry needed to sustain this family drama.
But a revival needs more than an impressive guest list, and this production never makes a convincing case that “Other Desert Cities” needed another trip to Broadway.
Alas, despite Baitz’s well-made play and an A-list cast, this revival is under-directed by John Benjamin Hickey, which leaves the actors feeling unmoored.
The family still feels more like chess pieces in Baitz’s strategic plot rather than fully rendered human beings who know each other deeply.

But here, director John Benjamin Hickey has chosen a path that strips Baitz's Pulitzer Prize finalist of its necessary nuance, so that even a late gut-punch plot twist loses its power to elicit gasps.
An absolute beast of a production , Other Desert Cities argues that some family stories demand to be told.
Other Desert Cities is most emphatically what Broadway does best, the kind of show where, on a single set, a quintet of actors gets to strut their stuff, guided by a supremely skilled writer.
Despite all the squabbling and acting out, family values still hold sway.
Other Desert Cities portrays the messy complexity of humans, and the ways by which even the people we know best can surprise us.

cn.t: Baitz's family drama remains timely and smartly written, with Lily Rabe earning particular praise, but the starry revival draws mixed reactions—some find it gutting and relevant, while others see an uneven, dated production coasting on celebrity casting.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored 1903 gem — one of the most gorgeous small theaters on Broadway. The 2017 renovation delivered some of the widest and most comfortable seats in the Theater District, with excellent sightlines from the intimate 970-seat house.

vr.q: Don't miss your chance to see this cast go toe to toe on a Broadway stage.
